baseRule: Employee state payroll taxes are modeled on FICA wages: gross pay minus Section 125 premiums, FSA, HSA, and commuter benefits, and not minus traditional 401(k). They are not subtracted from federal taxable wages. They are omitted for contractor mode because coverage is often optional.

programs.name: California SDI
programs.shortWhy: California disability and paid family leave, withheld from the employee. The 2026 rate is 1.3% with no wage ceiling.
programs.notes: Starting January 1, 2026 the worker contribution rate is 1.3% of wages. Senate Bill 951 removed the taxable wage ceiling beginning in 2024. This one withholding funds Disability Insurance and Paid Family Leave.

programs.name: New York disability (DBL)
programs.shortWhy: New York disability benefits. Withholding is 0.5% of wages but capped at $0.60 a week, $31.20 for the year.

source.name: New York State, disability benefits contribution cap

programs.notes: Employee contribution cannot exceed $0.60 per week. The annual maximum modeled here is $31.20.

programs.name: New York Paid Family Leave
programs.shortWhy: New York Paid Family Leave. For 2026 the employee rate is 0.432% of wages up to a $95,348.76 base, $411.91 maximum.

source.name: New York Paid Family Leave, 2026 rates

programs.notes: 2026 employee contribution rate 0.432%. The maximum annual contribution is $411.91, which is 0.432% of the statewide average weekly wage annualized to $95,348.76.

programs.name: Washington Paid Family & Medical Leave
programs.shortWhy: Washington paid leave. The 2026 employee share is about 0.808% of wages up to the $184,500 Social Security wage base.

source.name: Washington Employment Security Department, PFML premium rates

programs.notes: 2026 total premium is 1.13%. Employees pay 71.43% of the premium (about 0.808% of wages) and employers pay 28.57% (about 0.323%), up to the Social Security wage base. Small-employer exemptions from the employer share are not modeled; the employee share is still withheld.

programs.name: WA Cares
programs.shortWhy: Washington's long-term care premium. 0.58% of wages with no cap, unless you have an approved exemption. This estimate assumes no exemption.
programs.notes: The premium is 0.58% of gross wages with no wage cap. Workers with an approved exemption (including many who opted out during the original window, or who live outside Washington) do not pay it. This estimate cannot see an exemption, so it includes the premium.

programs.name: Oregon statewide transit tax
programs.shortWhy: A 0.1% statewide transit tax withheld from Oregon wages. There is no wage cap. It is separate from TriMet, which employers pay.

source.name: Oregon Department of Revenue, Statewide Transit Tax

programs.notes: Employee withholding of one-tenth of one percent has been in effect since July 2018 and remains 0.1%. TriMet and Lane Transit payroll taxes are employer excise taxes and are not in the employee stub.

programs.name: Colorado FAMLI
programs.shortWhy: Colorado paid family and medical leave. The 2026 employee share is 0.44% of wages up to the $184,500 Social Security wage base.
programs.notes: For 2026 the employee contribution is 0.44% up to the Social Security wage base, maximum $811.80. Employers with 10 or more employees pay a matching 0.44%. Smaller employers may owe no employer share; that exception is not modeled on the employer-cost tool.

programs.name: Connecticut Paid Leave
programs.shortWhy: Connecticut paid leave. Employees contribute 0.5% of wages up to the Social Security wage base.
programs.notes: The employee contribution rate is one-half of one percent of wages up to the Social Security contribution base. There is no employer premium in the standard plan.
